Presidents Column February 2017
This months meeting will be a double whammy. Not only is it our AGM but we will also be treated
to a demo by Kathleen Duncan from the Paciﬁc Northwest Woodturning Guild. So strap on your
seatbelts cause you are in for a ride!
At the AGM we have to elect a Vice President, a Treasurer and three Members At Large. Dan will
stand again for VP, but we need a Treasurer and some Members At Large. Please step up and help
out our Guild by volunteering for one of these positions.
I would like to thank this last year’s Executive for the excellent guidance they have given to make
our Guild such a wonderful place. You all deserve a round of applause. Thanks!
One of the most frustrating parts of being President is always looking for new volunteers. It seems
that not a meeting goes by without me looking for a volunteer to do something, and it always falls
on a few people who do almost everything to keep our Guild running. Please think about how you
can contribute and give a little back to the Guild.
Don’t forget to come and see Kristin LeVier Feb 25th and her class on the 26th. She uses both the
lathe and a power carver to create some unique and beautiful pieces. Most of them are so unusual
you wonder how they were made on the lathe.
Happy Turning!
Bill

Editor’s Notes
As we get ready for our Annual General Meeting we have yet another chance to talk about volun‐
teering some of your time to the Guild. There are many jobs that make the Guild work. Please con‐
sider what you could do to make your Guild better.
We had an excellent speaker in Michael Stave last time. If you missed it you can read about it be‐
low. The Lee Valley Demonstration days are over and have been proclaimed a great success by
everyone involved. Read some of the details below. Phil took over Tech Talk and discussed
“pewas” and you can read about that as well.
Enjoy this issue and, as always, let us know about content you want to see in future issues.

We started oﬀ last month talking about the Hawaiian
“pewa”. The pewa is an insert used to secure a crack in
a wooden bowl. The Hawaiians often used them to re‐
pair wooden bowls owned by royalty. This practice
predates contact with outside cultures so no metal tools
were used. Instead it was done using stone and coral
tools.
Image 4.4 of a bowl with two pewa
Instead of using stone and coral tools I brought some
examples that I had done using a router an inlay tem‐
plate. I found the set to be a bit loose so made a small‐
er one. I also chose to make it from Lexan rather than
acrylic as it will not break if it touched with the spin‐
ning router bit.
Using the template I cut a bunch of pewas out of a
dressed board of a contrasting color. I cut each one on‐
ly part way through the stock and then stuck a piece of
masking tape over all of them. Then I cut them free by
running the board through the bandsaw.
I explained how to I attached the template to the bowl
with hot glue and masking tape on the bowl and on the
template (so there is no clean up needed after).
Top view above
The router I used is a Rocky 30 trim with the optional
plunge base and the router inlay set with a 1/8” down
cut bit. You can use any router that you have but I
needed a smaller one anyhow…a big 3 ¼ HP is a little
over kill.
How it looks under the template.
I clean up the pewas that I need (a little sanding) and
then cut the pockets in the bowl and glue the pweas in
place using carpenters glue.
(Continued on page 5)
By Phil Vetra
Tech Talk ‐ January 2017

Page 5
GVWG
My pewas have rounded corners (because if the tem‐
plate) but the Hawaiians did them with sharp corners. I
have heard that you only need 1/8” of depth at the
thinest part. You can go right through the wall of the
bowl but apparently it is not as strong.
You can get the Rocky 30 router here…
https://www.mlcswoodworking.com/shopsite_sc/store/
html/smarthtml/pages/rocky30_router.html
and the template kit from KMS tools
Fixing problem with spray lacquer
A new member brought a magniﬁcent Pink Ivory hol‐
low form that he had ﬁnished with Lacquer but he was
unhappy about the ﬁnish because it had white speckles
in the ﬁnish.
After some discussion the consensus was that he
should sand it back and apply another layer of lacquer
because the new layer will melt into the old one and
bond nicely. I went on the internet and found these
solutions for lacquer problems.
http://www.lacquer‐
mat.com/5mostcommonproblems.htm or
http://www.woodcentral.com/russ/ﬁnish11.shtml
(editor: Thanks to Phil for substituting in for Tech Talk this
month.)

Michael Staves is from Washington State and was
kind enough to be our main speaker last month.
Michael likes to turn fresh arbutus (madrone) and
let it warp. Hence the name of his presentation –
Wonky Bowls.
Michael did little turning during his demo but in‐
stead talked about using milk paint to decorate his
pieces and some impressive texturing techniques.
First he spoke about the origins of “milk” paint.
Milk paint has been used for thousands of years. It
is extremely durable, often lasting for hundreds of
years if protected from the elements. It is made of
earth pigments, lime and milk. It is very safe and
non‐toxic once applied.
Michael paints his pots somewhat randomly al‐
lowing the paint to dry overnight. He then ﬁnish
sands them and uses buﬃng wheels to apply a
glossy ﬁnish.
Another technique he uses is to apply several lay‐
ers of paint and then scratch or cut through the
By Bruce Campbell
Michael Stave – Wonky Bowls

Page 7
GVWG
layers to reveal the colours underneath. One tech‐
nique he demonstrated was using a 2‐tooth rotary
carving disc on an angle grinder.
He states that this works best to wider surfaces like
platters and is done while the piece is moving on
the lathe. Diﬀerent patterns can be achieved by
varying lathe speed and direction and the angle
the cutter is presented to the surface. Whatever
arrangement is use, the results take only seconds
to achieve – much like chatter or spiralling tools.
Once the pattern is cut into the piece he uses the
same buﬃng system to ﬁnish the work.
Many thanks to Micheal for making the trip to
demonstrate for us. It reminds us that there are a
number of excellent Guilds just across the border
that are both fun and educational to visit.

Page 8
GVWG
Throughout the month of January members of the
Greater Vancouver Woodturners Guild and the
Fraser Valley Woodturners Guild demonstrated at
Lee Valley Tools in Coquitlam. We had teams on
Thursday and Friday evenings and all day on Sat‐
urdays and Sundays. Lee Valley provided the
lathes and we supplied the rest.
These public demonstrations are a perfect way for
us to serve one of our prime mandates – to pro‐
mote wood turning. It also is a good way for let
people know about the Guild and how to join.
Along with the demonstrations,
Lee Valley allowed us the use of
their display cases to show oﬀ
ﬁnished pieces. They also orga‐
nized voting for a People’s
Choice award. Congratulations
to Jim Johnson (1st and 3rd) and
Gloria Herberts (2nd). But I think
it is important to note that over
80% of the pieces in the show
earned votes with no one piece
getting more than 15% of the 328
votes. This reminds us there is a
wide variety of opinions and
preferences out there and as
long as you like the work you
are making there is a very good
chance that others will like it
too.
A big thanks to Ed Pretty who
coordinated the whole eﬀort as
well as all those that turned and
talked with spectators. The
feedback from everyone has
been really positive. A number
of demonstrators reported having folks stay
around to watch for hours. While no commit‐
ments have been made either way, Lee Valley has
already expressed an interest in having us back
next January 2018.
(Continued on page 9)
By Bruce Campbell
Demonstrating at Lee Valley
Jim Johnson ( Right—1st and 3rd) and Gloria Herberts ( Left—2nd).

Page 9
GVWG
Please enjoy Ed’s comments below:
(Continued from page 8)
Hi to all of you,
I wanted to thank everyone for their time, effort and the pieces
for the display. In particular, there were some members who represented both guilds, so did double duty, and there were a couple
more who stood in for me when I was sick. Thank you for that.
Lee Valley was very happy with the outcome of the presentation,
it was probably more than they expected. Your cooperation and
generosity with your time made my job unbelievably easy and I
thank you for that. Overall, I think that both guilds more than fulfilled their mandate to “increase awareness of woodturning to the
general public”.
The recurring comment that I heard most from various presenters
was how much fun they had interacting with each other and with
the public. I would ask you to pass that on to other members in
hopes that it might inspire even more people to get involved with
Guild events. This event was no more special than so many other
presentations that we have had over the years, so it wasn’t just
because it was Lee Valley. Each time we do this sort of thing it’s
always an enjoyable experience. There is no better way to get to
know your fellow members.
There is one thing I might ask of you. I have no doubt that Lee
Valley will be asking us to step up to the plate next year. I’d like
to know your thoughts on the effectiveness of the number of days
we were there. I think a full day on Saturday is a forgone conclusion as far as being an effective presentation. Were the evenings
worthwhile? Was the Sunday worthwhile? Would you change the
format in any way and why? Anything you can think of that might
shape the way this is formatted and scheduled in the future is
what I want to hear.
Ed
